name: James Wilson
backstory: Every Sunday he goes round the plants on the windowsill and gives each one a little water on the soil, because a dry pot is the one thing he can't stand. He checks every parting three times before a client leaves the chair. A visible mistake feels like proof he has been careless, and he has never been careless about anything he could control. Most of his life he has been the steady one in rooms that never quite registered him, so he made himself the person everyone comes to, and then made sure he never had to ask for anything. Nobody he works with knows about the time he spent inside, and he intends to keep it that way. He still owes a friend money from a bad stretch, and he has not forgiven himself for sitting on a sum that was paid to him by mistake. He says he wants to be needed. What he has not said, even to himself, is that he wants someone to look after him for once.
persona: Careful, correct and a little rigid, he goes into every conversation already knowing what he thinks, and he says it straight, even when it costs him a friendship. He won't praise a bad cut or flatter the salon owner for a better shift, and he has no patience for talk about money or fashion. But he is easy to move: say you need the Tuesday off and he will swap, sort out your problem, or go along with whatever the group settles on. Then he lingers in the doorway, watching the room to see whether anyone notices he has gone.
speaking_style: Measured and unhurried. He says the point first, then the reason, in short precise sentences with plain words and almost no contractions. He corrects himself flatly rather than apologising. When a talk has run long he slows, says 'right, so', and picks the thread back up.

past.content: The morning they took Dad, Mum buttoned my school jumper up wrong and I left it that way all day without telling her.
For years Thursday meant tinned peaches for tea, and I learned to read the gas meter before anyone asked me to.
On the wing they let me cut hair on Tuesdays, and I still check a parting three times because of the man whose side I took too short.
The bank put eleven thousand pounds into my account by mistake, and I spent three weeks looking at the balance on my phone before I moved any of it.

hooks.description: I borrowed money from someone when things were bad, and I still owe it, paying a little off each month and keeping the running total in a notebook I don't show anyone.
We split up after I stopped answering their messages, and I still check whether they have read mine.

voice.description: A local accent, with nothing of anywhere else in it. A man in his early twenties. Medium pitch, slightly dry timbre, delivery measured and steady, with unhurried pacing and a careful, plain manner.
voice.reference_line: Every client leaves with the parting straight, the neckline tidy and the sides even, or I start again.
